A graph is a data structure consisting of nodes, also called vertices, and edges, also called connections, that link pairs of nodes together. Graphs model relationships and networks of all kinds. Social networks are graphs. Road maps are graphs. Computer networks are graphs. Dependencies in projects are graphs. Knowledge bases are graphs. Unlike trees, which have no cycles, graphs can be cyclic and disconnected. Graphs are classified as directed, where edges have a direction, or undirected, where connections are bidirectional. They can be weighted, where edges carry numeric values, or unweighted.

Fundamental concepts matter. A node represents an entity. An edge represents a relationship between two nodes. In a directed graph like Twitter follows, edges have direction. In an undirected graph like roads connecting cities, edges are bidirectional. In a weighted graph, edges carry numeric labels representing distance, cost, or some other metric. The degree is the number of edges connected to a node. In directed graphs, there's an in-degree and an out-degree.

Graphs come in common types. An acyclic graph has no cycles and is used for dependency graphs and scheduling. A connected graph has a path between any two nodes. A complete graph has an edge between every pair of nodes. A bipartite graph splits nodes into two groups with edges only between groups, useful for matching problems.

There are multiple ways to represent graphs in memory. An adjacency matrix is a two-dimensional array where the element at position i j indicates an edge from i to j. This works well for dense graphs but takes O of n squared space. An adjacency list uses an array of lists where each node stores its neighbors. This is efficient for sparse graphs, taking O of n plus m space where m is the number of edges. An incidence list lists edges directly instead of adjacencies, which is useful for weighted graphs.

Key algorithms operate on graphs. Breadth-first search, or BFS, explores level by level and finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search, or DFS, explores as far as possible and can detect cycles and perform topological sorting. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path in weighted graphs with non-negative edges. Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms compute the minimum spanning tree, connecting all nodes with minimum total weight.

Graphs are one of the most versatile data structures in computer science. Almost every real-world network is modeled as a graph—the internet, transportation systems, biological pathways, and recommendation engines. Understanding graph algorithms is essential for backend engineers, data scientists, and anyone working on optimization, routing, or relationship modeling. The problem of finding an efficient path through a graph or determining feasibility appears in countless practical applications, from GPS navigation to compiler optimization to social network analysis. Graph algorithms are a major algorithm family. Trees are special acyclic types of graphs. Data structures like arrays and linked lists are fundamental alongside graphs. Some graph algorithms use divide-and-conquer strategy. Shortest-path problems are solved using dynamic programming. And Big O notation is critical for analyzing graph algorithm complexity.
